newsitem.title: USA: NYC to get 35 pct of state school aid - paper.
newsitem.headline: NYC to get 35 pct of state school aid - paper.

text.p: New York City stands to get 35.13 percent of $11 billion of state aid for schools, the Daily News reported Monday.

The paper quoted Assembly Education Committee Chairman Steven Sanders, D-Manhattan, as saying that city schools would get about that percentage, up one-quarter of a one percent, from last year's share. However, the new rate still would fall short of the city's share of the state's school children, which stands at 37.8 percent, the paper said.
The News added that the final budget includes $428 million for child care, a 30 percent rise over last year.

Separately, the New York Times reported Monday that Gov. George Pataki signed a proposed $2.4 billion school bond that will be submitted to voters on the November ballot. The city was expected to get approximately $1 billion of this bond, if voters approve the act.

Other measures that were approved by the legislature, which over the weekend began approving the state's new, 1998 fiscal budget, included $130 million for a new, 750-cell prison in Altamount, near Tupper Lake in the Adirondacks, the paper said.

The bill also includes funds to build 800 maximum security cells for unruly prisoners, at eight existing prisons. A new "merit time" progam for prisoners who were convicted of nonviolent crimes, would let them cut by one-sixth the minimum term of their sentences if the finished special work and treatment programs, the Times said.

The state's approximately $67 billion budget, which set a new record for tardiness as it was due on April 1, included 500 new drug treatment beds and 250 shelter beds for victims of domestic violence.

New York City's tax break for unincorporated businesses also was approved. The proposal would give business owners' a tax credit on their city income tax, costing the city about $74 million a year, the Times said.

New York City Mayor Giuliani had pressed for this credit, though he opposed another approved by the legislature that the Republican governor has yet to sign, the paper said. This bill would require independent hearing officers to be appointed to handle serious disciplinary cases involving municipal workers.

Another bill approved by both houses aimed to raise the number of elderly in managed care programs to 50,000 from the present 2,500, by letting more companies provide such services as home-care and nursing homes.

An agreement was reached to extend the New York Racing Assocation's franchise for running horse-racing tracks at Aqueduct in Queens, Belmont in Nassau County, and Saratoga Springs, until 2007, the Times said.
The paper added a deal appeared close on redrawing six Congressional districts in New York City to comply with a federal appellate court ruling.

And the lawmakers were expected to approve bills requiring health insurance companies to cover almost unlimited chiropractic services, and set a two-year window during which hemophiliacs, who had gotten H.I.V. from a blood product, to sue the manufacturers.

Further, lawmakers gave themselves $150 million to spend on a variety of local projects, the paper said, citing $583,000 for the Saratoga Performance Arts Center, at the request of State Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy.
